summary: Defines how an operator might use part of the MPLS header to encode Explicit Congestion Notification marks. It builds on RFC 3270. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: ECN is a way for a router to say to the sender of a packet that the network is congested, without throwing the packet away. MPLS networks had no way to carry that signal, because the only spare field is three bits wide and is already used for the traffic class. This RFC works out how to squeeze the signal into what is left and how to check at the edge of the network that the receiver will understand it.

questions: how does ecn work in mpls
what is the mpls exp field used for
subtitle: Carrying congestion marks in the three-bit EXP field of an MPLS label, without wasting codepoints.

tldr.problem: Explicit Congestion Notification lets a router tell a sender to slow down instead of dropping a packet, but MPLS networks had no way to carry that mark, because the only spare field is three bits wide and already holds the service class.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns congestion codepoints per traffic class inside the EXP field, so that each class that uses marking spends two codepoints, one unmarked and one marked, and the egress router of each domain checks whether the transport can handle the mark.
tldr.outcome: ECN works end to end across MPLS networks, the scheme extends to pre-congestion notification, and the document is explicit about the one cost: a packet that cannot be marked may be carried to the edge of the domain before being dropped there.

facts.label: Codepoints per behaviour using ECN
facts.value: At least two: not congested and congested

facts.label: Drop rate from bit overloading
facts.value: 0.15% for 6 LSRs each marking 1% of packets

facts.label: PCN states
facts.value: Three: admission marked, termination marked, not marked

facts.label: Where the transport is checked
facts.value: At the egress routers of the MPLS domain

today: RFC 5129 is a Proposed Standard and its EXP field was later renamed by RFC 5462, which renamed it the Traffic Class field. The scheme it defines, per-domain ECN capability checking at the edge of the MPLS domain, is the one described here, and the appendix on pre-congestion notification remains an illustration of how the mechanism extends to schemes that need more than two states.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification for IP has as its primary purpose the signalling of congestion without dropping packets. The Diffserv architecture in MPLS networks is defined with a way of encoding Diffserv code points in an MPLS header, and DSCPs may be encoded in the EXP field, while other uses of that field are not precluded. The earlier document makes no statement about how Explicit Congestion Notification marking might be encoded in the MPLS header, and this document fills that gap.

There is a consequent interest in being able to support ECN across IP networks consisting of MPLS-enabled domains, because pre-congestion notification is being developed for admission control and flow termination. It is therefore necessary to specify the protocol for including ECN in the MPLS shim header and the protocol behaviour of edge MPLS nodes.

ECN for IP uses four codepoints, encoded in two bits of the IP header. The MPLS EXP field is the logical place to encode ECN codepoints, but with only 3 bits, 8 codepoints, available, and with the same field being used to convey DSCP information as well, there is a clear incentive to conserve the number of codepoints consumed for ECN purposes. The document also notes that ECN for IP defines default usage of the ECN field but allows for the possibility that some Diffserv per hop behaviours might include different specifications on how the ECN field is to be used, and it seeks to preserve that capability.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS has one small field in its label that can carry extra information, and it is usually used for the traffic class. This RFC works out how to also put a congestion mark in that field without running out of room.

sections.title: The Terms Used Here
sections.content:
The document draws on the terminology of ECN and MPLS and repeats a few definitions. Congestion Experienced is one of the states with which a packet may be marked in a network supporting ECN. A packet is marked in this state by an ECN-capable router to indicate that this router was experiencing congestion at the time the packet arrived.

ECN-capable Transport is one of the ECN states a packet may be in when it is sent by an end system. An end system marks a packet with an ECT codepoint to indicate that the endpoints of the transport protocol are ECN-capable. A router may not mark a packet as Congestion Experienced unless the packet was marked ECT when it arrived. Not ECN-capable transport is the state in which an end system marks a packet to indicate that the endpoints of the transport protocol are not ECN-capable. A congested router cannot mark such packets as Congestion Experienced, and thus it can only drop them to indicate congestion.

The EXP field is a 3-bit field in the MPLS label header that may be used to convey Diffserv information and, in this document, ECN information. Penultimate Hop Popping is an MPLS operation in which the penultimate label switching router on a label switched path removes the top label from the packet before forwarding the packet to the final label switching router on the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Three terms matter. ECT means the sender and receiver can both handle congestion marks. Congestion Experienced is the mark itself. Not ECN-capable means the pair cannot, so the only thing a router can do is drop the packet.

sections.title: Using the EXP Field for ECN
sections.content:
Label switching routers configured for explicit congestion notification should use the EXP field in the MPLS shim header. Because the earlier Diffserv document already defines use of codepoints in the EXP field, and the field is only 3 bits, the space available for ECN is clearly limited.

That earlier document defines two approaches for requesting differentiated service treatment from a label switching router. In the EXP-Inferred-PSC approach, different codepoints of the EXP field indicate the packet's per hop behaviour. In the Label-Only-Inferred-PSC approach, an MPLS label is assigned for each scheduling class, so that a router determines both its forwarding and its scheduling behaviour from the label. If a domain uses the label-only approach there is likely to be space in the EXP field for ECN codepoints, whereas with the EXP-inferred approach the codepoint space is likely to be scarce. The document focuses on interworking ECN marking with the EXP-inferred approach, as it is the tougher problem, and says the same approach can also be applied with label-only paths.

The recommendation is that explicit congestion notification in MPLS should use codepoints instead of bits in the EXP field. Since not every per hop behaviour will necessarily require an associated ECN codepoint, it would be wasteful to assign a dedicated bit for ECN. For each behaviour that uses ECN marking, one EXP codepoint is defined as not congestion marked and at least one other codepoint is defined as congestion marked, so each such behaviour consumes at least two EXP codepoints, while behaviours that do not use ECN marking consume only one.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than one bit for congestion, this RFC spends a whole code value per traffic class: one value for normal, one for congested. Traffic classes that never use congestion marking spend nothing extra. The approach is designed for the harder case, where the EXP field already carries the class.

sections.title: Per-Domain ECT Checking
sections.content:
The egress nodes of an MPLS domain are defined as the nodes that pop the last MPLS label from the label stack, exposing the IP or, potentially, non-IP header. Such a node may be the ultimate or the penultimate hop of a path, depending on whether penultimate hop popping is employed.

In the per-domain ECT checking approach, the egress nodes take responsibility for checking whether the transport is ECN-capable. The document does not specify how these nodes should pass on congestion notification, because different approaches are likely in different scenarios, but if congestion notification in the MPLS header is copied into the IP header the procedure must conform to the specification given. If congestion notification is passed to the transport without first being passed onward in the IP header, the approach used must take similar care, and if the transport for a particular congestion marked MPLS packet is found not to be ECN-capable, the packet must be dropped at this egress node.

Only the egress nodes check whether an IP packet is destined for an ECN-capable transport. Therefore any single label switching router within an MPLS domain must not be configured to enable ECN marking unless all the egress routers surrounding it are already configured to handle ECN marking. A domain surrounded by ECN-capable egress routers is called an ECN-enabled MPLS domain. The term only implies that all the egress routers are ECN-enabled; some interior routers may not be, so it is possible to use legacy routers incapable of supporting ECN in the interior of a domain as long as all the egress routers are ECN-capable. If penultimate hop popping is used, the routers that perform the pop operation do need to be ECN-enabled, since they act in this context as egress routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The check happens once, at the point where the packet leaves the MPLS domain and its IP header becomes visible again. Interior routers may mark optimistically. The rule is that marking cannot be enabled anywhere inside the domain unless every egress router is ready to check.

sections.title: What Each MPLS Node Does
sections.content:
When an IP packet is encapsulated with an MPLS label stack, the ECN field must be translated from the IP packet into the MPLS EXP field. The not congestion marked state is set in the EXP field if the ECN status of the IP packet is Not-ECT, ECT(1) or ECT(0), and the congestion marked state is set if the ECN status of the IP packet is Congestion Experienced. If more than one label is pushed at one time, the same value should be placed in the EXP value of all label stack entries.

When one or more labels are pushed onto an MPLS labelled packet, the EXP field is copied directly from the topmost label before the push to the newly added outer label, and if more than one label is pushed the same EXP value is copied to all label stack entries.

If the EXP codepoint of a packet maps to a per hop behaviour that uses ECN marking, and the marking algorithm requires the packet to be marked, the congestion marked state is set, irrespective of whether it is already in that state. If the buffer is full, a packet is dropped.

If an MPLS-encapsulated packet crosses a Diffserv domain boundary, the two domains may use different encodings of the same behaviour in the EXP field, in which case the EXP field must be rewritten at the boundary, and the appropriate ECN marking should also be preserved. If an MPLS-encapsulated packet in the congestion marked state crosses from an ECN-enabled domain to a domain that is not ECN-enabled, the egress checking procedures must be performed at the egress router of the ECN-enabled domain, which means that if the encapsulated packet is not ECN-capable it must be dropped. That implies the egress router must be able to look beneath the MPLS header without popping the label stack.

When a packet has more than one MPLS label in the stack and the top label is popped, another MPLS label is exposed, and the ECN information should be transferred from the outer EXP field to the inner label. If the inner EXP field is not congestion marked it is set to the same state as the outer field, and if the inner EXP field is congestion marked it remains unchanged whatever the outer field. An inner value of congestion marked and an outer value of not congestion marked should be considered anomalous and should be logged in some way by the router.

When the last MPLS label is popped the payload is exposed. If that packet is not IP and does not have any capability equivalent to ECT, it is assumed not ECN-capable and treated as such, so if the EXP value is congestion marked the packet must be dropped. Assuming an IP packet was exposed, a Not-ECT packet must be dropped if the EXP field is congestion marked. If the ECN information is to be transferred from the MPLS header into the exposed IP header for onward transmission, and an operator chooses to do so, the ECN field of the inner packet remains unchanged if the EXP field is not congestion marked, and is set to Congestion Experienced if the EXP field is congestion marked.
sections.plainLanguage: At each router the mark is carried along, and when a congested router wants to mark a packet it does so regardless of what it already says. When the last label comes off and the IP header reappears, the router checks: if the sender could not have handled a congestion mark, the packet is dropped there and then.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The first deployment question is what happens when a packet that is not ECN-capable gets marked. The problem only arises if there is congestion downstream of an earlier congested queue in the same MPLS domain. Congested routers downstream might forward packets already marked, even though they will be dropped later when the inner IP header is found to be Not-ECT on decapsulation, and such packets might cause the downstream routers to mark or drop other packets that they would otherwise not have had to.

Congestion will typically be rare in MPLS networks, but it might not be. The extra unnecessary load at downstream routers will not be more than the fraction of marked packets from upstream routers, even in the worst case where no transports are ECN-capable. That is why the per-domain ECT checking approach was chosen: the most likely effect is a very slightly increased marking rate, resulting in very slightly higher drop only for non-ECN-capable transports. The alternative was rejected because it introduced a low but persistent level of unnecessary packet drop for all time, even for ECN-capable transports. A partial solution would be to preferentially drop packets arriving at a congested router that were already marked.

The second question is what happens if some legacy routers in the domain cannot support ECN. If they are used in the interior this is not a problem: they simply have to drop packets if they are congested rather than mark them, which is the standard behaviour for IP routers that are not ECN-enabled. If a legacy router were used as an egress router it would not be able to check the ECN-capability of the transport correctly, so an operator in that position must not enable ECN unless all egress routers are ECN-capable.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a small cost. A packet that will be thrown away anyway may travel to the edge of the domain first, and other packets may be marked because of it. The RFC accepts that cost because the alternative drops a steady trickle of packets for every flow, including the ones that can handle marks.

sections.title: Example Uses
sections.content:
The first example is the straightforward one. ECN for IP proposes the use of ECN in TCP, with the ECN-Echo and Congestion Window Reduced flags in the TCP header. ECN could be enabled in an MPLS domain for per hop behaviours such as assured forwarding and best effort that are expected to be used by TCP and similar transports, so that end-to-end congestion control in capable transports could respond to approaching congestion without relying on packet discard.

The second example is co-existence with differentiated services networks built on the EXP-inferred approach, which many operators have deployed. In many cases the number of behaviours used is less than 8, so codepoints remain available. To support ECN for a single behaviour, an operator can allocate a second codepoint to that behaviour for the congestion marked state and keep the old codepoint for the not congestion marked state. An operator with only four deployed behaviours could enable ECN marking on all of them. As an illustrative example, an operator using aggregated service classes might support ECN only for one aggregate, using the EXP codepoint 010 for the not congestion marked state and 011 for the congestion marked state.

The third example is congestion-feedback-based traffic engineering, in which an egress router feeds congestion back to an ingress router so that flows can be shifted to an alternate path, using a new Resource Reservation Protocol message sent by the egress router to the ingress router and ignored by transit routers.

The fourth example is pre-congestion notification, which proposes using marking on routers within an edge-to-edge Diffserv region to control admission of new flows and to terminate existing flows in response to disasters and other anomalous routing events. If routers are able to mark packets to signify congestion in MPLS, that marking could be used for admission control and flow termination across a Diffserv region, whether it contained pure IP routers, MPLS routers, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism can be used for the obvious purpose, signalling congestion to TCP. It can also be used to steer traffic around a congested path, and to warn a whole region before it becomes congested so that new flows can be refused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document believes no new vulnerabilities are introduced by it. It has considered whether malicious sources might exploit the fact that interior routers will mark packets that are Not-ECT, relying on the egress router to drop them. Although this might allow sources to engineer a situation where more traffic is carried across an MPLS domain than should be, the reasoning is that even without this feature those sources would have been able to prevent the routers dropping that traffic anyway, simply by setting ECT in the first place.

The document also notes that an ECN sender can use the ECN nonce to detect a misbehaving receiver, and that the nonce works correctly across an MPLS domain without requiring any specific support from this proposal, since it does not need to be present in the MPLS shim header. If there were a need for an ECN nonce in the MPLS shim header, the proposal does not preclude the later addition of such a capability for specific code points.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is exposed here. The document considers whether a sender could cheat by pretending to be capable of handling congestion marks, and concludes that such a sender could already achieve the same effect.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH ROUTER DOES WITH THE MARK

items.title: Push a label onto an IP packet
items.text: The ECN field is translated into the EXP field: not congested unless the packet was already marked congested.

items.title: Push another label
items.text: The EXP field is copied from the topmost label to the new outer label.

items.title: Congestion at an interior router
items.text: The congested state is set if the marking algorithm asks for it, whatever the packet already said. If the buffer is full the packet is dropped.

items.title: Pop a label with more labels left
items.text: The state moves from the outer label to the inner label.

items.title: Pop the last label
items.text: A packet that cannot handle a congestion mark, or is not IP at all, must be dropped if the label says congested.

viz.caption: AN ILLUSTRATIVE USE OF TWO EXP CODEPOINTS

items.label: Not-CM
items.desc: The EXP codepoint used for the not congestion marked state of the Assured Elastic Treatment Aggregate.

items.label: CM
items.desc: The EXP codepoint used for the congestion marked state of the same aggregate.
